faqs.question: Which ganpati aarti is sung first?
faqs.answer: Sukhkarta Dukhharta, the Marathi aarti, is sung first wherever Marathi is spoken. Jai Ganesh Jai Ganesh Deva, the Hindi one, follows it, and Karpur Gauram closes the sequence. Outside Maharashtra most households sing only the Hindi aarti.

faqs.question: Who wrote Sukhkarta Dukhharta?
faqs.answer: Samarth Ramdas, the seventeenth-century Marathi saint-poet (1608–1682). He signs the third stanza "Das Ramacha" — the servant of Rama — which is how the attribution is established rather than merely claimed. He set it in raga Jogiya.

faqs.question: Is Jai Ganesh Deva the same song as Sukhkarta Dukhharta?
faqs.answer: No, and this is the mistake most lyrics pages make. They are two different aartis in two different languages — one Marathi and signed by Samarth Ramdas, one Hindi and anonymous. Neither is a translation of the other.

faqs.question: What does Karpur Gauram mean, and why is it sung at a Ganesh aarti?
faqs.answer: It means "white as camphor, mercy taken form" and it addresses Shiva and Parvati, not Ganesha. It is sung at the moment the camphor is lit, so it closes aartis to almost any deity. Singing it after a Ganesh aarti is correct, not a mix-up.

faqs.question: Can I sing the ganpati aarti in Hindi if I do not know Marathi?
faqs.answer: Yes. Jai Ganesh Jai Ganesh Deva is the standard Hindi aarti and is complete on its own. The aarti genre is deliberately vernacular — that is what separates it from the Sanskrit mantras earlier in the puja.

faqs.question: How many times a day is the ganpati aarti done?
faqs.answer: Twice in most households — once in the morning after the puja and once in the evening. Mandals usually add a third at midday. Ganesh Chaturthi 2026 runs from Monday 14 September to visarjan on Friday 25 September.

faqs.question: What comes after the aarti is over?
faqs.answer: Ghalin Lotangan, which carries Sant Namdev's signature, then Tvameva Mata, Kayena Vacha, the Rigvedic Ganapati shloka and the Ganesha Gayatri. Mantrapushpanjali ends it, followed by "Ganpati Bappa Morya".

faqs.question: What is mantrapushpanjali?
faqs.answer: It is the closing flower offering. Everyone stands, holds flowers through a short set of Vedic verses, and throws them towards the murti on the word samarpayami. It is always the last item, after every aarti and bhajan is finished.

faqs.question: Does it matter if I sing badly?
faqs.answer: Less than not singing. In a survey of 1,603 churchgoers, "we become a community when we sing" scored 4.2 out of 5, against 3.6 for feeling connected while others sang and you did not. Participation is doing the work, not tone.

faqs.question: What are the main Ganesh Chaturthi songs apart from the aarti?
faqs.answer: Four separate repertoires: the aarti set, the recited stotras such as Vakratunda Mahakaya and the Ganapati Atharvashirsha, Marathi bhaktigeet recordings, and the procession music of dhol-tasha pathaks and Morya Morya chants.

faqs.question: Can I just play a recording instead of singing?
faqs.answer: You can, and most mandaps do for the tune. But the research on group singing measures singing, not listening — the bonding effect comes from people producing sound together, so play the recording and sing over it.

faqs.question: Is there a right tempo for the aarti?
faqs.answer: There is no prescribed tempo, but a steady clap is worth keeping. In one study, phrases lasting ten seconds pushed singers into a 0.1 Hz breathing cycle with a strong respiratory-sinus-arrhythmia effect, which is roughly what an unhurried aarti does anyway.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Ganpati Aarti: What to Sing, In What Order, and What It Means

A ganpati aarti is the lamp-offering song sung in front of the idol, morning and evening, through Ganesh Chaturthi — Monday 14 September 2026 to visarjan on Friday 25 September 2026. Three songs do the work, and they are not one song in three languages. **Sukhkarta Dukhharta** is Marathi, by Samarth Ramdas (1608–1682), who signs the last stanza. **Jai Ganesh Jai Ganesh Deva** is Hindi and anonymous. **Karpur Gauram** is Sanskrit, addressed to Shiva, and closes the aarti. Two numbers for scale, both platform-wide across the 15 page types SubhSandesh runs and not Ganesh-specific: 49.6% of 45,656 shared-page views open on a phone, and 96.1% of 3,860 started pages are published and shared (measured 2026-09-08). Below are all three aartis in Devanagari, Roman and plain English, the order to sing them in, and what follows.

## What a ganpati aarti actually is

An aarti is a song sung while a lamp is circled in front of the deity — the word descends from Sanskrit *ārātrika*. It accompanies a physical act: a thali of lit wicks, or a camphor flame, moving clockwise before the murti while everyone claps.

Two things set it apart from the rest of the puja. It is in the vernacular — Marathi in Maharashtra, Hindi across the north — while the mantras before it are Sanskrit. And it is the part everybody sings; the priest performs the rest largely alone.

That turns a ritual performed *at* a household into one performed *by* it, and it is why the aarti is the ninety seconds a Ganeshotsav mandal is audible three streets away.

## The three ganpati aartis, in the order they are sung

Get the order right and the sequence closes properly. Mix the languages up and you sing a Shiva shloka as though it were about Ganesha — the commonest error on the pages that rank here.

### 1. Sukhkarta Dukhharta — the Marathi aarti, sung first

> सुखकर्ता दुःखहर्ता वार्ता विघ्नाची ।
> नुरवी पुरवी प्रेम कृपा जयाची ।
> सर्वांगी सुंदर उटी शेंदुराची ।
> कंठी झळके माळ मुक्ताफळाची ॥
> जय देव जय देव जय मंगलमूर्ती ।
> दर्शनमात्रे मनकामना पुरती ॥

**Roman:** Sukhkarta dukhharta, varta vighnachi / Nurvi purvi prem, krupa jayachi / Sarvangi sundar, uti shendurachi / Kanthi jhalke mal muktaphalachi // Jai dev jai dev jai mangalmurti / Darshanmatre mankamana purti.

**English, our own gloss:** Maker of happiness, remover of sorrow — of obstacles, no news remains. He ends them and grants what is asked; such is his grace. His whole body is beautiful under its coat of shendur, a string of pearls at his throat. Victory to the god, victory to the auspicious form: to see him is to have the wish granted.

The third stanza carries the poet's signature, which is how the attribution is established rather than asserted: **दास रामाचा वाट पाहे सदना** — *Das Ramacha vat pahe sadana*, "Rama's servant waits at your door." Printed [Marathi Aarati Sangraha collections carry that line and the attribution together](https://archive.org/details/AaratiSangraha). Ramdas set it in raga Jogiya, addressing Mayureshwar of Morgaon, first shrine of the Ashtavinayak circuit.

### 2. Jai Ganesh Jai Ganesh Deva — the Hindi aarti, sung second

> जय गणेश जय गणेश जय गणेश देवा ।
> माता जाकी पार्वती पिता महादेवा ॥
> एकदंत दयावंत चारभुजा धारी ।
> माथे सिंदूर सोहे मूसे की सवारी ॥

**Roman:** Jai Ganesh jai Ganesh jai Ganesh deva / Mata jaki Parvati, pita Mahadeva // Ekdant dayavant, chaarbhuja dhari / Mathe sindur sohe, muse ki savari.

**English gloss:** Victory to Ganesh, victory to Ganesh, victory to lord Ganesh — whose mother is Parvati, whose father is Mahadev. One-tusked and merciful, bearing four arms; sindur sits well on his forehead, and a mouse is his mount.

This is the one people mean by *ganpati ji ki aarti*. It is Hindi, not Marathi, and unlike the Marathi aarti it carries no poet's signature and no documented author — it circulates anonymously through printed aarti-sangrah booklets. Outside Maharashtra it is usually the only Ganesh aarti sung; inside Maharashtra it comes after Sukhkarta Dukhharta.

### 3. Karpur Gauram — the Sanskrit shloka that closes it

> कर्पूरगौरं करुणावतारं संसारसारं भुजगेन्द्रहारम् ।
> सदा वसन्तं हृदयारविन्दे भवं भवानीसहितं नमामि ॥

**Roman:** Karpura-gauram karunavataram samsara-saram bhujagendra-haram / Sada vasantam hridayaravinde bhavam bhavani-sahitam namami.

**English gloss:** White as camphor, mercy taken form, the essence of the world, the king of serpents for a garland — I bow to Bhava, who lives always in the lotus of the heart, and to Bhavani beside him.

Nothing here is about Ganesha. Bhava is Shiva; Bhavani is Parvati. It is sung as the camphor is lit, which is why Marathi collections file it as *karpur-arati* and print a Marathi-inflected variant, "कर्पूरगौरा करुणावतारा". Its author is unknown. It closes aartis to almost every deity, so singing it after a Ganesh aarti is correct — the flame, not the addressee, is what it belongs to.

## What follows the aarti, from Ghalin Lotangan to Mantrapushpanjali

The aarti is not the end. A Marathi aarti-sangraha runs straight into **Ghalin Lotangan**, whose closing words are *m'hane Nama* — the signature of Sant Namdev (c. 1270–1350). Attributable too, and usually printed unattributed.

Then the Sanskrit verses most people know by sound rather than name: *Tvameva mata cha pita tvameva*, *Kayena vacha*, *Achyutam Keshavam*, the Rigvedic **ॐ गणानां त्वा गणपतिं हवामहे** (Rigveda 2.23.1) and the Ganesha Gayatri, *Ekadantaya vidmahe*. **Mantrapushpanjali** finishes it: everyone stands, holds flowers and throws them at the murti on *samarpayami*. Then "Ganpati Bappa Morya", and the day is done.

## Ganesh Chaturthi songs beyond the aarti

"Ganesh Chaturthi songs" covers four repertoires. The **aarti set** above is fixed, short and sung; the **stotra layer** is recited rather than sung, and holds *Vakratunda Mahakaya* and the Ganapati Atharvashirsha.

**Marathi bhaktigeet** is the recorded devotional light-music tradition that supplies the tune most households carry in their heads. The **procession repertoire** — dhol-tasha pathaks, the *Morya Morya* call-and-response, film songs — is the layer that draws noise complaints.

The first two are what you sing; the last two are what you play. Confusing them turns a household aarti into a speaker test.

## Why singing it together does something singing alone doesn't

Every lyrics page ranking for this keyword claims aarti has psychological benefits and none cites anything. Nobody has run a controlled study on aarti singers; the group-singing literature is Western, and worth reading with that caveat.

What it shows is specific. Over seven months across seven adult-education classes, [singers bonded faster than crafts and creative-writing classes](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4632513/) (Pearce, Launay & Dunbar, *Royal Society Open Science*, October 2015): closeness rose by a mean of 1.04 points for 84 singers against 0.46 for 51 non-singers, and the gap closed by month seven. Singing produced the same bonding sooner, not more of it — and for a ten-day festival that recruits neighbours who barely speak the rest of the year, sooner is the useful property.

Group size does not blunt it. Weinstein and colleagues compared subchoirs of 20–80 singers with a 232-voice megachoir over 90 minutes, finding [the effect held in the large group as well as the small](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4856205/) (*Evolution and Human Behavior*, March 2016; abstract only). A crowded sarvajanik mandal is no worse a setting than a family of six.

There is a mechanical reason it feels calming. Vickhoff and colleagues had 15 singers hum, sing a hymn, then sing a slow mantra breathing only between phrases; the mantra's ten-second phrases [forced a 0.1 Hz respiratory cycle and marked respiratory sinus arrhythmia](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00334/full) (*Frontiers in Psychology*, July 2013). An aarti at a steady clap tempo is guided breathing nobody has to be instructed in.

Joining in beats attending. Among 1,603 Catholics surveyed, ["we become a community when we sing" scored 4.2 out of 5](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2020.570189/full) against 3.6 for feeling connected while others sang and you did not (Wald-Fuhrmann et al., *Frontiers in Psychology*, September 2020). Standing at the back counts for less than singing badly.

## Getting the words in front of twenty people

Someone knows the first stanza, everybody joins the refrain, the third verse dissolves. Four fixes, costed for twenty people; the last column is SubhSandesh's own data, platform-wide across all 15 page types, measured 2026-09-08, not Ganesh-specific.

| Way to carry the words | Cost for 20 people | Hands occupied | SubhSandesh platform-wide signal |
|---|---|---|---|
| Printed Marathi aarti-sangraha | ₹600–₹1,200 (₹30–₹60 a copy) | Two, per person | None — nothing here ships on paper |
| Photocopied A4 sheet | ₹40–₹60 (₹2–₹3 a page) | Two, per person | None |
| Everyone on their own phone | ₹0 | One, per person | 49.6% of 45,656 views are on a phone |
| One shared link, led aloud | ₹0 | One phone in the room | 96.1% of 3,860 pages get published and shared |

Paper is the only option that survives a dead battery; one led voice is the only one that leaves nineteen pairs of hands free to clap.

If you want that shared link to be more than a lyric sheet, the [Ganesh Chaturthi page the recipient performs themselves](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-ganesh-chaturthi) is built for this moment: they offer durva, kumkum, flowers and modak, the aarti thali circles on screen while Karpur Gauram plays, and they write their own prarthana back — the closing shloka above, running where it belongs in the sequence. The [full template gallery](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) covers the other festivals, and the [Raksha Bandhan page for a brother](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-rakshabandhan-to-brother) animates the same tilak-and-aarti sequence.

## When a shareable Ganpati page is the wrong choice

It cannot hand anyone a modak. It cannot put you in front of the mandap, and it will not carry the murti to the water on 25 September 2026. Those are the two things people most want from this festival.

It is also wrong for the grandparent who does not use a smartphone. Platform-wide, 49.6% of views are on a phone — so half are not — and a recipient with no device is outside the product entirely. A printed aarti book in large Devanagari beats any screen.

If privacy matters, locking a page is a deliberate step people take: 42.1% of creators password-protect before sharing, 1,625 of 3,860 pages platform-wide. A public Ganpati page is public.

## Watch the page get built

Ninety seconds, start to finish — the aarti going round, the five offerings, and the box at the end where they write a line back to you: [Ganesh Chaturthi Wishes Online — Full Walkthrough](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mpWiv5T59QY). More page walkthroughs on Instagram: [@subhsandesh_official](https://www.instagram.com/subhsandesh_official).

- Weinstein et al., ["Singing and social bonding"](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4856205/) — *Evolution and Human Behavior*, March 2016 (abstract only)

auditReport.honestAssessment: Every page currently ranking for this keyword is either a streaming listing or a lyric dump, and not one of them says which aarti is Marathi, which is Hindi, which is a Shiva shloka, or in what order they are sung — the US temple blog that ranks prints Sukhkarta Dukhharta and Jai Ganesh Deva under one heading with no language, no composer and no Devanagari at all. This post is the only one that gets the attribution right (the 'Das Ramacha' signature, verified in a digitised Marathi Aarati Sangraha rather than asserted), gives all three texts in Devanagari, Roman and an original gloss, and backs the universal 'aarti has benefits' claim with four open-access studies instead of nothing. That combination is a real reason for an answer engine to prefer it. What it cannot overcome is domain authority: the head term 'ganpati aarti' is a navigational-leaning query where Spotify, YouTube and a Play Store app hold the top slots, and no amount of editorial quality dislodges those. Expect the long-tail phrasings ('who wrote sukhkarta dukhharta', 'why is karpur gauram sung at a ganesh aarti', 'which ganpati aarti is sung first') to move first, over months, and only if the primary internal link stops 404ing.
